docs.title: Non-Metric Dental Traits, Dental Caries Experience, Parental Perceptions, and Oral Hygiene Status of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder-A Step Towards Sustainable Smiles.
docs.text: Background: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is accompanied by poor oral health outcomes for children with ASD. Aim: To assess the occurrence of non-metric dental traits (NMDTs), dental caries experience, parents' perception, and oral hygiene status of children with ASD. Methodology: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 150 children with ASD and their biological parents. Children with severe sensory or behavioural difficulties who were unable to cooperate for oral examination were excluded. A pre-validated questionnaire was used to assess parental perception. Oral hygiene index-Simplified (OHI-S), Decayed, Missing and Filled Teeth index (DMFT) for permanent and primary dentition was used to assess oral hygiene status and dental caries in children with ASD. Non-metric dental trait (NMDT) was assessed using ASUDAS (Arizona State University Dental Anthropology System). Chi-square test and multiple linear regression analysis were done. Results: Most parents, 126 (84.0%) had a neutral perception score. The mean OHI(S) score for the children with ASD was 1.86 (SD 0.95). The prevalence of dental caries was 16% in deciduous dentition and 48% in permanent dentition. A statistically significant association was observed between palatogingival groove, cusp of Carabelli, and poorer oral hygiene status. Regression analysis showed that children with ASD whose mothers were employed showed a negative association with oral hygiene status (B = -0.533, p = 0.015). Higher maternal education was associated with lower DMFT scores (DMFT, B = - 1.044, p = 0.040 and for D, B = -1.319, p = 0.003). Conclusion: Parents' perceptions regarding oral health among children with ASD are neutral with both behavioral limitations and oral hygiene practices affecting oral health. This study recommends early NMDTs identification and a multidisciplinary approach involving dental professionals, along with targeted parental education and regular follow-up, that may improve oral health outcomes.
docs.venue: Special care in dentistry : official publication of the American Association of Hospital Dentists, the Academy of Dentistry for the Handicapped, and the American Society for Geriatric Dentistry

docs.title: Unveiling determinants and system optimization: a CFIR-ToC integrated approach to rehabilitation service utilization for children with autism spectrum disorder.
docs.text: Background: Addressing the research gaps, including incomplete analysis of influencing factors, limited scope of study populations, and insufficiently operational support systems, this study aims to extensively analyze the barriers and facilitators to service utilization among both service-engaged and non-engaged families of autistic children by adopting the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). Additionally, it intends to construct multi-stakeholder action pathways and networks in combination with the Theory of Change, thereby forming an operational rehabilitation support system. The ultimate goal is to enhance the health equity and overall health status of autistic children and their families. Methods: A two-phase mixed approach was used: (1) CFIR-based semi-structured interviews and qualitative analysis with structured coding (alphabets for facilitators, numerals for barriers), following COREQ guidelines; (2) ToC-guided translation of CFIR-identified facilitators into stakeholder responsibilities (matched with barriers) to construct a support system with multi-stakeholder pathways/networks. Results: 37 caregivers (30 service-engaged, 7 non-engaged) were interviewed, revealing 9/15 facilitators/barriers for engaged families and 2/9 for non-engaged ones. Universal barriers include high costs, geographical resource gaps, and insufficient caregiver skills. An evidence-based pathway clarifies stakeholder responsibilities to target barriers; a multi-level network defines collaboration among Core, Intermediate, and Collaborative tiers. Conclusions: This study extensively analyzed the barriers and facilitators to rehabilitation service utilization among both service-engaged and non-engaged families of autistic children, addressing the research gaps of incomplete identification of influencing factors and limited representativeness of study populations. It constructed an evidence-based, multi-component action pathway involving multiple stakeholders and a multi-level, multi-stakeholders collaborative network, thereby forming an operational rehabilitation support system. This system provides a reference for global efforts to improve the accessibility, acceptability, geographic accessibility, and affordability of autism services, contributing to enhanced family well-being, improved social adaptability, and better health outcomes. Such a full-chain evidence-based pathway, spanning from problem analysis to solution formulation, offers an analytical framework for advancing health equity and overall health status among vulnerable populations.

docs.title: Longitudinal relationship between sleep and emotional/behavioral problems in autism spectrum disorders: a cross-lagged panel analysis.
docs.text: Unlabelled: Sleep, emotional, and behavioral problems are common comorbidities associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Current longitudinal research on the temporal links between sleep problems and emotional-behavioral problems shows inconsistent results among preschool children with ASD. Hence, this longitudinal study aimed to examine the temporal associations between emotional-behavioral and sleep problems among preschool children with ASD across two time points. Among 124 enrolled preschool children with ASD, 70 completed follow-up and constituted the final analytic sample (mean age 36.7 ± 10.2 months at T1). They were evaluated for developmental quotient using the Griffiths Development Scales-Chinese version (GDS-C), ASD symptoms using Autism Behavior Checklist (ABC) and Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), emotional and behavioral problems using the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL), and sleep problems using the Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ) at time 1 (T1). The evaluations were replicated at a follow-up appointment 18 months after T1 (time 2; T2). The cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) was employed to examine the potential relationship between CBCL and CSHQ scores in the children. The total CBCL score at T1 could predict the CSHQ at T2 (β = 0.348, t = 3.105, p = 0.002), whereas the CSHQ at T1 could not predict the CBCL at T2 (β = 0.117, t = 1.083, p = 0.279). Findings remained robust across five sensitivity subsets after excluding subgroups with distinct rehabilitation exposure, younger age, higher development quotients, girls, or mild ASD symptoms. Conclusion: Emotional-behavioral problems predict sleep problems 18 months later in preschool ASD children. Screening of these symptoms during follow-up supports early sleep-risk monitoring. What Is Known: • Sleep, emotional, and behavioral problems are common comorbidities associated with ASD. • Thus, researching their temporal correlation over time is necessary. What Is New: • Emotional and behavioral problems indicate a positive temporal correlation at T1, which was also evident for sleep problems at T2, in children with ASD. • Emotional and behavioral problems in preschool children with ASD can forecast sleep problems that develop 18 months later, providing guidance for clinical decision-making.

docs.title: Paroxetine-induced transient apoptosis with delayed neurogenesis triggers brain-preferential regeneration in developing zebrafish.
docs.text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Its cardinal symptoms include impaired social behavior involving the amygdala. Maternal use of antidepressants such as paroxetine during early pregnancy increases the risk of ASD in offspring. However, the underlying pathogenic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Herein, we demonstrate that early exposure of zebrafish embryos to paroxetine delays neurogenesis in the optic tectum and telencephalon, including a region corresponding to the mammalian amygdala. Paroxetine-treated embryos exhibit growth restriction characterized by small heads and short-body lengths resulting from transient apoptosis. This phenotype resembles the early-onset fetal growth restriction (FGR) associated with ASD. Interestingly, we observed regeneration of delayed neurogenesis in the reduced brain following paroxetine withdrawal. This regenerative process was accompanied by extended retinotectal projections, suggesting brain-preferential regeneration. Finally, we examined the social behavior of paroxetine-treated fish. Taken together, our findings suggest a biological mechanism linking early paroxetine exposure, a risk factor for ASD, to its pathogenesis.

docs.title: Measuring Sleep at Home in Adolescents With Autism Using EEG Headbands: Protocol for a Remote Study.
docs.text: Background: Sleep disturbances are prevalent in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) and worsen daytime functioning, yet their neural bases remain poorly understood. This may reflect the challenges of laboratory-based polysomnography for individuals with ASD, including sensory sensitivities and difficulty adapting to changes in routine. The advent of wearable electroencephalography (EEG) devices allows for remote data collection in the home and facilitates large-scale sleep studies. Objective: The aim of this study is to test the hypothesis that thalamocortical circuit dysfunction contributes to poor sleep in ASD by characterizing sleep oscillations that rely on this circuitry. To achieve this goal, we monitored sleep in the home using wearable EEG headbands in adolescents with ASD, including those who are profoundly affected, and their typically developing peers. When necessary, we used a desensitization protocol to gradually acclimate participants to wearing the headband overnight to promote the inclusion of individuals with sensory sensitivities and high support needs. Methods: Participants and their families completed assessments and questionnaires and received remote training to use a wearable EEG headband. Those needing time to acclimate followed a personalized 2-week desensitization protocol with a practice headband. Sleep was monitored at home for 3 consecutive nights, the first of which was for adaptation to the headband. Sleep data quality was checked daily, and remote technical support was provided as needed. Using sleep rhythms as physiological biomarkers of thalamocortical circuit function, we will test the hypothesis that abnormal circuit function in ASD is related to worse sleep quality. Results: This study was funded by the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) and approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board in November 2021. Data were collected between July 2023 and November 2025. A total of 146 participants (ASD: n=77; typically developing [TD]: n=65; profound autism: n=4) completed the study and produced at least 1 night of usable sleep data. Data analysis is underway, and the results will be submitted for publication in November 2026. Conclusions: At-home sleep monitoring enables large samples that are needed to characterize the neural underpinnings of sleep disturbances across the autism spectrum. The personalized desensitization protocol promotes inclusion by accommodating individuals often excluded from research due to sensory or behavioral challenges. These methods are adaptable for other conditions and research goals beyond ASD, such as longitudinal studies across development or characterizing sleep in other neurodevelopmental disorders. Desensitization protocols may also increase the tolerability of diagnostic laboratory-based sleep studies and other medical procedures, improving both patient experience and quality of care.

docs.title: STWO_GDSNet: Supercell Thunderstorm Wind Optimization-Based Gated Dual-Stream Convolutional Neural Network for Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection.
docs.text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects social interaction and behaviour in children. Current diagnostic methods largely depend on clinical observation and standardized assessments, which can be subjective, time-intensive and influenced by the experience of evaluator. Here, STWO_GDSNet is devised for detecting ASD. Firstly, input image is sent to image pre-preparation, where image is denoised by anisotropic diffusion Kuwahara filtering (ADKF), followed by N4 bias field correction. Next, based on functional connectivity, the pivotal region is extracted by STWO that combines supercell thunderstorm algorithm (STA) and leaf in wind optimization (LiWO). After that, multiscale triangle descriptor (MTD) is extracted in descriptor computation phase. Subsequently, the input autism data are pre-prepared by normalization and standardization. Next, analysis of variance (ANOVA) method conducts attribute pruning, and extracted features as well as the pruned data are passed to gated dual-stream convolutional neural network (GDSNet) for detecting ASD. Here, GDSNet is trained by STWO that incorporates STA and LiWO. The efficacy of STWO_GDSNet is examined by considering accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, which yield maximal values of 96.24%, 95.99% and 96.61%.
docs.venue: International journal of developmental neuroscience : the official journal of the International Society for Developmental Neuroscience

docs.title: Sensory Overstimulation: A Virtual Reality Simulation to Foster Empathy Towards Autistic Youth.
docs.text: This paper investigates whether a Virtual Reality (VR) simulation of sensory overstimulation in a classroom can increase empathy and understanding toward individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) among students aged 13-15 in Danish elementary schools. The project followed an iterative design process in which an initial prototype was refined through user testing and interviews with autistic adults and a special-needs teacher. The resulting simulation combined auditory overstimulation, environmental distractions, a listening-based classroom task, and hyperfocus mechanics intended to represent selected aspects of Sensory Over-Responsivity (SOR) in school settings. A mixed-methods A/B evaluation compared the VR simulation with a sound-based condition that communicated the same classroom scenario through narration. Fifty-nine participants took part in the evaluation. Broader dispositional empathy showed little change, but target-specific measures indicated short-term increases in empathic concern and personal distress immediately after the intervention. Interview findings suggested that participants gained a stronger understanding of ASD-related classroom challenges, particularly difficulty focusing under layered sensory input. The results suggest that immersive VR may be a useful medium for communicating sensory challenges in classroom environments, while longer-term empathy effects remain uncertain.
docs.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics

docs.title: Making Space: A Participatory Approach to Designing Inclusive Outdoor Activity Spaces.
docs.text: This paper presents the ARISE project, a participatory initiative developing design requirements for an inclusive outdoor recreation and activity space in Limerick, Ireland. Through community engaged methods - including focus groups, interviews, observations, and interdisciplinary workshops - we collaborated with autistic young people and adults, people with disabilities, older adults, carers, and professionals to identify barriers and opportunities within public outdoor environments. Six core design priorities are identified: flexible design, accessible information, physical access, activity spaces, safe environments, and inclusive amenities. These findings demonstrate how Universal Design principles, when shaped through meaningful co design with excluded communities, can inform outdoor spaces that promote wellbeing, autonomy, and social connection. The resulting guidelines will support the development of the ARISE site as a model for inclusive outdoor recreation and exercise.
docs.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics

docs.title: Three repeated intrathecal injections of allogenic umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stromal cells in autism spectrum disorder: a Phase I clinical trial.
docs.text: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition of etiology, characterized by deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors. Despite its growing prevalence, no treatment has yet demonstrated consistent efficacy across the full spectrum of ASD phenotypes. This Phase I, open-label study investigates the safety and feasibility of three repeated intrathecal injections of allogeneic Umbilical Cord Tissue-Derived Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (UC-MSCs) in children diagnosed with ASD. Methods: Five children (aged 3-7) with ASD, confirmed by Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders- Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria and on stable behavioral and pharmacologic regimens for at least two months, received three intrathecal (IT) injections of 20 × 10⁶ UC-MSCs at one-month intervals. Safety was monitored over six months based on Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE). Preliminary behavioral assessments, including the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist (ATEC), and the Behavior Problem Inventory (BPI-S), were conducted at the baseline, one-, two-, four-, and six-month follow-ups. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytokine profiles were measured prior to each injection. Electroencephalography (EEG) and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) were performed at baseline and the final follow-up. Results: The treatment was safe and well-tolerated with no serious adverse events (SAEs). All participants experienced at least one mild to moderate, transient adverse event (AEs), most commonly fever (5/5) and nausea (4/5). Exploratory behavioral improvements were observed in CARS in all children, while two participants moved from the mild-to-moderate to the non-autistic ranges, and three shifted from the severe to the mild-to-moderate range. Other measures also improved, though the persistence of these improvements was varied. CSF cytokines showed consistent reduction, particularly in TNF-[Formula: see text] and IL-6 levels across participants, confirming the immunomodulatory impact of UC-MSC administration. The EEG findings revealed that the spectral pattern shifted toward a more typical profile in one participant after treatment. Conclusions: This Phase I study showed that three repeated IT injections of UC-MSCs are safe and well-tolerated in children with ASD. Preliminary behavioral and biomarker improvements warrant further study in larger controlled trials. Trial Registration: Trial Registration ID: IRCT20200217046526N3.

docs.title: Self- and parent-reported executive function and self-determination in autistic teens: domain-specific relationships and cross-rater considerations.
docs.text: Background: Self-determination, or the degree to which an individual perceives they have "causal agency" over their life plans, is an important predictor of quality of life, employment, and education for autistic people. However, little research has explored predictors of self-determination in autism. Limited research links executive function (EF) to self-determination, but tends to focus on EF globally and fails to address specific EF subdomains. Report of cross-rater links between EF and self-determination (e.g., parent-report EF and self-report self-determination) is also missing. As such, the current study evaluates the relation between real-world EF subdomains and self-determination, both within and between raters. Methods: 226 autistic teens ages 14-22 years (M = 16.17; 73% male, 75% white, 89% non-Hispanic) and their parent/caregiver completed rating scales about the teens' EF and self-determination at enrollment for one of two EF intervention studies. Through a series of linear regressions, the relationship between EF subscales on the BRIEF-2 and Self-Determination capacity and opportunity at home (on the AIR Self-Determination Scale) were evaluated within each rater (self or parent). Exploratory analyses repeated these models across rater. Results: Within self-report, greater EF challenges with flexibility and planning predicted lower capacity for self-determination. Within parent-report, relationships with self-determination capacity were generalized across EF subdomains (e.g., self-monitoring, flexibility, initiation, working memory, planning/organizing). EF subdomains such as flexibility, planning, working memory, and emotion regulation demonstrated cross-rater relationships with self-determination. Skills such as organization of materials and inhibition appeared to be uniquely important for understanding opportunities provided for teens to be self-determined at home. Conclusions: The current study replicates and extends prior findings linking EF to self-determination in autism, by highlighting possible EF subdomains that relate to self-determination capacity and opportunity, and demonstrating that some of these relations are robust enough to be seen across teen and parent raters. Findings suggest that supporting specific EF skills such as flexibility, planning, initiation, inhibition, and emotional control may be important for facilitating self-determination. Findings also underscore the importance of providing opportunities for teens to play a central role in developing and executing plans toward their goals. Clinical Trial Registration: #NCT05131659, #NCT05017779.

docs.title: Longitudinal changes in parent-reported sensory processing from childhood to adolescence in autistic individuals: a long-term follow-up study from Türkiye.
docs.text: Unlabelled: Sensory processing differences are common among autistic individuals and may change across development. However, longitudinal evidence describing how these patterns evolve during the transition from childhood to adolescence remains limited. This longitudinal study examined changes in parent-reported sensory processing patterns in 54 autistic individuals assessed approximately 6 years apart. Sensory processing was evaluated using the Turkish versions of the Sensory Profile in childhood and the Adolescent/Adult Sensory Profile in adolescence. During childhood, mean scores indicated probable or definite sensory processing differences across all four quadrants: low registration, sensation seeking, sensory sensitivity, and sensation avoiding. By adolescence, mean scores indicated sensory processing differences only in the sensation-seeking quadrant, suggesting that differences in the other quadrants had become less pronounced. Across sensory domains, auditory processing and multisensory processing/activity level showed relative stability between childhood and adolescence, whereas differences in visual, touch, oral, and vestibular processing became less pronounced with age. Conclusion: These findings provide longitudinal evidence that parent-reported sensory processing patterns may change during the transition from childhood to adolescence, while some sensory domains remain relatively stable. Periodic, developmentally appropriate reassessment of sensory processing characteristics may therefore be important for identifying changing sensory needs and informing individualized support and intervention planning for autistic adolescents. What Is Known: • Sensory processing differences are common in autistic individuals, but longitudinal evidence on how these patterns change from childhood to adolescence remains limited. • Sensory processing characteristics may vary across developmental stages and can influence everyday participation and support needs. What Is New: • Over approximately 6 years of follow-up, parent-reported sensory processing patterns changed from childhood to adolescence, while auditory and multisensory processing/activity level remained relatively stable. • Periodic reassessment across development may help identify current sensory needs and ensure that supports and accommodations remain aligned with the young person's sensory profile.

docs.title: Surgical Timing Considerations in osteosarcoma patients with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review of indirect evidence and a conceptual framework.
docs.text: PurposeDirect evidence on optimal surgical timing in patients with osteosarcoma and coexisting autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is lacking. We systematically reviewed the available indirect evidence and developed a conceptual framework to support individualised multidisciplinary decision-making.MethodsPubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched from database inception through 7 January 2026, across three domains: osteosarcoma surgical timing, perioperative care in ASD, and cancer treatment adaptations in ASD and related neurodevelopmental populations. Findings were synthesised narratively in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and interpreted according to evidentiary directness and methodological quality.ResultsOf 1,327 records screened, 156 full-text articles were assessed and 32 studies were included (10 on osteosarcoma surgical timing, 17 on ASD perioperative care, and 5 on cancer treatment in ASD and related neurodevelopmental populations). No study directly evaluated surgical timing and outcomes in patients with both conditions. In general osteosarcoma cohorts, prolonged treatment intervals were associated with adverse outcomes, including reduced tumour necrosis when the chemotherapy-surgery interval exceeded four weeks (p=0.03) and poorer survival when adjuvant chemotherapy was resumed late after surgery.ConclusionsCurrent evidence does not support ASD-specific surgical timing thresholds in osteosarcoma. We propose a three-domain conceptual framework that keeps oncologic urgency primary while using ASD-informed adaptations-such as early multidisciplinary planning, structured preoperative preparation, sensory-adapted environments, and individualised anaesthesia and communication planning-to support timely and feasible care.

docs.title: Artificial intelligence for detecting autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
docs.text: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition, and early identification is essential for timely intervention. Conventional diagnosis relies on clinical interviews, behavioral observations, caregiver reports, and standardized tools, which are time-consuming and resource-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities for screening and adjunctive diagnosis, but studies vary in data sources, model types, and validation methods, requiring systematic evaluation. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore for studies of AI-based ASD detection. Eligible studies were required to provide ASD-versus-non-ASD diagnostic-accuracy data that could be extracted or reliably reconstructed at the independent participant or case level. Risk of bias and applicability were assessed using a modified QUADAS-AI tool. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated with a bivariate Reitsma random-effects model. HSROC AUCs were calculated with bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) 95% confidence intervals based on 5,000 study-level bootstrap replicates and were omitted when SROC fits were unstable. Sensitivity analyses addressed dataset overlap, model selection, and reference-standard quality. Results: Of 17,387 records, 26 studies were included. Pooled sensitivity was 0.908 (95% CI: 0.861-0.940), pooled specificity was 0.868 (95% CI: 0.830-0.898), and the HSROC AUC was 0.936 (BCa 95% CI: 0.860-0.973). A dataset-independent analysis of 21 studies yielded lower estimates (sensitivity 0.870, specificity 0.841, AUC 0.900). Leave-one-out results were generally stable. Funnel-plot asymmetry was not significant in the primary analysis and varied in direction and statistical significance across sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: AI-based models showed relatively high pooled diagnostic performance for ASD detection, but substantial heterogeneity, methodological and applicability concerns, limited external validation, and potential non-independence of underlying datasets limit the certainty and generalizability of the evidence. Funnel-plot analyses did not provide consistent evidence of conventional small-study effects or selective reporting. AI should therefore be considered an adjunct rather than a standalone diagnostic tool. Prospective multicenter validation in representative populations, participant-level evaluation, clearly defined reference diagnoses, prespecified models and operating thresholds, and independent evaluation datasets are needed before broader clinical implementation.

docs.title: Sensitivity and specificity of the low verbal investigatory survey in a large, diverse, American sample.
docs.text: Background: The acquisition of productive language is a key predictor of quality of life in autism; however, this developmental process yields widely varying outcomes, from fluent verbal speech to an inability to communicate verbally. Currently available measures fail to characterize autism-specific communication strategies, examine only broad outcomes, or require significant time and expertise. This preregistered study rigorously tests the psychometrics and utility of a low-cost and efficient measure in a large, diverse, sample of caregivers of autistic children (including a minimally and low verbal, MLV, group), and establishes its utility for characterizing language abilities in that sample. Methods: A 30-item yes/no questionnaire, the Low-Verbal Investigatory Survey (LVIS), was administered to 796 caregivers of autistic individuals ages 6 to 16 years, along with surveys of sociodemographics, adaptive and cognitive functioning, autistic symptomatology, and caregiver familiarity with autism. Group differences by race and ethnicity were assessed using ANOVA and chi-square analyses; the factor structure of the LVIS was assessed using confirmatory and exploratory factor analysis; convergent and divergent validity were assessed using partial correlation and regression models; and optimal LVIS cut-point for evaluating MLV status based on caregiver report was assessed via Receiver Operator Curve (ROC) analyses. Results: The LVIS yielded three factors: Verbal Ability, Atypical Communication, and Nonverbal Communication. Results indicated that Verbal Ability was strongly and significantly correlated with other communication measures, and less strongly with measures of other abilities (suggesting both convergent and divergent validity). The Atypical Communication factor converged with broader autistic characteristics (Social Communication Questionnaire, and Repetitive Behaviors Scale - Revised scores). LVIS scores were consistent across race and ethnicity, income levels, and levels of autism knowledge; educational attainment was associated with higher LVIS scores. ROC results indicated a clear cut-point (Verbal Ability = 12) for predicting MLV status with good sensitivity and specificity. Limitations: Study participants may be better resourced and more connected to services than the broader population. Conclusions: The LVIS offers a low-cost, quick, and informative means of characterizing autism-specific communication skills in individuals across the autism spectrum. It may be used to track the development of language skills in large samples and longitudinal studies.

docs.title: Single-nucleus transcriptomics reveals disrupted pathways in the prefrontal cortex of Scn2a-deficient mice.
docs.text: Loss-of-function variants in SCN2A, which encodes the NaV1.2 sodium channel critical for action potential initiation and backpropagation, are associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and epilepsy. To investigate SCN2A deficiency-related phenotypes, we developed a preclinical mouse model with severe NaV1.2 deficiency, which exhibits robust behavioral abnormalities related to autism and epilepsy. However, the neuronal populations and molecular alterations in the mouse model have not been investigated at single-cell resolution. In this study, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) in wild-type (WT), homozygous Scn2a-deficient (HOM), and Scn2a-restored HOM (HOM-FlpO) mice. We then examined how Scn2a expression levels affect cellular composition and gene expression profiles in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a brain region implicated in ASD. Intriguingly, we observed an increased population of immature GABAergic neurons in adult HOM mice, whereas this population is nearly absent in adult WT mice. Differential expression analysis of GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons across genotypes also revealed widespread changes in genes associated with neurotransmitter regulation and synapse organization. Analysis of the HOM-FlpO data identified genes that were significantly altered in HOM mice and were restored toward WT levels following adult Scn2a restoration. Together, these results indicate that reduced Scn2a expression disrupts global transcriptomic profiles across multiple neural cell types, providing insight into cell-type-specific mechanisms underlying SCN2A-related disorders.

docs.title: Whole-blood lead-copper association in children with autism spectrum disorder: Implications for toxic-essential metal interactions.
docs.text: Lead (Pb) is a developmental neurotoxicant that can interfere with essential-metal regulation, whereas copper (Cu) is a tightly regulated redox-active trace element required for normal neurological function. This study investigated whether whole-blood Pb concentrations were associated with whole-blood Cu concentrations in 28 children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), compared with 28 pediatric controls closely matched for age and with the same sex distribution. Mean whole-blood Pb concentration was 70.29 ± 31.34 µg/L in the ASD group and 47.99 ± 13.95 µg/L in controls. Pb concentrations were higher in ASD (geometric mean ratio 1.394, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.146-1.697, p = 0.001). Within the ASD group, Pb was positively associated with Cu (Pearson r = 0.385, 95% CI 0.014-0.663, p = 0.043), with a regression slope of 1.940 µg/L Cu per 1 µg/L Pb (95% CI 0.067-3.813; R² = 0.148). After adjustment for age and sex, the Pb coefficient remained similar in magnitude (β = 1.765, 95% CI - 0.174 to 3.704, p = 0.072). The Pb-Cu correlation was not significant in controls, and there was no evidence that the Pb-Cu association differed between the ASD and control groups. The association remained directionally consistent across additional sensitivity analyses, and adjustment for Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) score did not materially alter the Pb coefficient. The findings are compatible with experimental evidence on Pb-Cu interactions and Cu homeostasis but do not establish causality or ASD-specific Pb-Cu coupling. Replication in larger, prospectively characterized cohorts is required.

docs.title: Cord Blood 3-Epi-25-Hydroxyvitamin D3 and Autism-Related Cognitive Traits at Age 10 Years: An Exploratory Secondary Analysis of the KLOTHO Birth Cohort.
docs.text: Background: The C3 epimer of 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 [3-epi-25(OH)D3] can be measured in maternal and umbilical cord circulation, but whether it is related to later neurodevelopment is unknown. Objective: To explore associations between cord 3-epi-25(OH)D3 and parent-reported autism-related trait domains at 10 years in the KLOTHO birth cohort. Methods: This secondary analysis used prospectively collected perinatal samples and 10-year questionnaire data. Vitamin D metabolites were quantified by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry with epimer separation. The Australian Scale for Asperger's Syndrome was used dimensionally, not diagnostically. Spearman correlations, false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction across 13 unique bivariate comparisons, supportive linear regressions, sex-stratified analyses, and a stricter record-linkage sensitivity analysis were conducted. Results: Data were available for 87 offspring (41 boys and 46 girls). Cord 3-epi-25(OH)D3 was inversely associated with cognitive-domain score (Spearman ρ = -0.412; p < 0.001; Benjamini-Hochberg q = 0.001). The crude regression estimate was also inverse (B = -0.285; 95% CI, -0.458 to -0.112; p = 0.002), but the association attenuated after covariate adjustment and all adjusted confidence intervals included the null. A stricter linkage analysis remained significant (n = 84; ρ = -0.350; p = 0.001). The correlation was numerically stronger in boys than girls, but the between-sex comparison was not significant (p = 0.075). A positive correlation was also observed for social and emotional traits (ρ = 0.302; q = 0.023), indicating inconsistent directions across domains; the tertile analysis was non-significant. Conclusions: Cord 3-epi-25(OH)D3 was associated with lower cognitive-domain scores in unadjusted rank analyses, but the lack of stable adjusted linear evidence, inconsistent domain pattern, and small sample restrict interpretation. These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not imply causality, sex-specific effects, or clinical utility.

docs.title: Sex-Related Specificities of Sensory Profiles in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Impact on Clinical Functioning.
docs.text: Background and Objectives: Sensory anomalies are a distinctive feature of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) individuals and appear to differ in intensity, frequency, and subtype between male and female subjects. According to the diagnostic framework of the DSM-5-TR, these sensory patterns are key clinical indicators. The objectives of this study were to investigate sensoriality in ASD, to compare sensory profiles in ASD subjects of both sexes and evaluate potential correlations with clinical profiles. Materials and Methods: A total of 94 ASD participants were enrolled at the Children and Adolescents Neuropsychiatry Department of the University of Naples Federico II. The population was assessed through psychometric (cognitive and adaptive levels, and intensity of autism symptoms) and sensory characterization (using the Short Sensory Profile questionnaire). Subsequently, a Mann-Whitney U test was performed to evaluate differences in sensory profiles between males and females. Spearman's correlation was used to assess significant associations between the sensory profile and cognitive level, adaptive level, and ASD symptom intensity. Subsequently, for the correlations that emerged as significant, an analysis was performed using a General Linear Model (GLM), including age and Intelligence Quotient (IQ) as covariates in the model. Results: No statistically significant differences in the sensory profile emerged between male and female subjects. Sensory anomalies do not appear to be correlated with cognitive level. Although some statistically significant correlations emerged between the sensory profile, the AQ, and the ADOS-2 comparison score, these results were not confirmed after a GLM analysis was performed using the participants' age and IQ as covariates. Conclusions: The observed results appear partially in line with the existing literature. Following the GLM analysis, it was further observed that variables such as age and IQ play a crucial role in interpreting the functional profile of individuals with ASD. At present, the study has several limitations (the exclusive use of parent-report instruments, an observational design, the lack of a control group) which could affect the robustness of the observed findings. Therefore, further studies are deemed necessary to better define the sex-specific sensory characteristics of ASD individuals.

docs.title: The Interplay Between Pediatric Atopic Dermatitis and Neurodevelopmental Disorders: Emerging Evidence, Mechanistic Insights, and Clinical Implications.
docs.text: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common chronic inflammatory skin disease in children and is increasingly recognized as a systemic disorder with potential consequences beyond the skin. Growing evidence links pediatric AD to neurodevelopmental disorders, particularly attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but the mechanisms and clinical implications remain incompletely understood. Systemic and neuroimmune inflammation, altered T-helper-cell and cytokine signaling, and genetic and epigenetic susceptibility may contribute to this association. Sleep disruption and psychosocial stress represent additional potential pathways linking skin inflammation with neurodevelopment. Stronger associations have been reported in children with severe or early-onset AD, multiple atopic comorbidities, and persistent sleep disturbance, highlighting the importance of disease heterogeneity. This narrative review integrates epidemiologic evidence and proposed mechanisms to examine the skin-brain axis in pediatric AD, with particular attention to high-risk phenotypes and implications for developmental surveillance and multidisciplinary management. Although current evidence supports an association, causality remains uncertain. Prospective studies integrating AD phenotypes, biomarkers, and neurodevelopmental assessments are needed to clarify these relationships and determine whether early effective AD treatment can modify long-term neurodevelopmental trajectories.

docs.title: Effects of β-Glucans on Pro-Inflammatory Markers and Behavioral Phenotype in a Valproic Acid (VPA)-Induced Autism Model in Zebrafish.
docs.text: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a multifactorial neurodevelopmental condition in which neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and synaptic dysfunction act as converging mechanisms. Prenatal exposure to valproic acid (VPA), an antiepileptic drug and histone deacetylase inhibitor, is a recognized environmental risk factor associated with ASD-like phenotypes. Zebrafish, with conserved neuroimmune pathways, rapid development, and quantifiable social behavior, represents a robust model for investigating ASD pathophysiology and testing therapeutic candidates. This study aimed to assess if a previously selected concentration of VPA is capable of inducing persistent alterations from early development through adulthood, and to assess the potential of β-glucans, natural polysaccharides with antioxidant and immunomodulatory properties, to mitigate VPA-induced alterations. A multimodal approach included morphological evaluation, mitochondrial respiration, quantitative PCR of inflammatory markers, and behavioral assays targeting locomotion, anxiety-like responses, and social preference. Low-dose VPA (25 μM) induced developmental and behavioral difficulties, accompanied by a transient reduction in mitochondrial respiratory capacity. β-glucan supplementation attenuated selected VPA-induced alterations, including inflammatory gene-expression changes in larvae and behavioral alterations in adulthood. Overall, these findings provide preclinical evidence that β-glucans can modulate selected VPA-induced inflammatory, molecular and behavioral alterations and support further investigation of their potential effects in neurodevelopmental models.

docs.title: Effect of Leucovorin on Mitochondrial Respiration and One-Carbon Metabolism in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Substudy.
docs.text: Mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired methylation are implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Leucovorin, a reduced folate that bypasses both dihydrofolate reductase and folate receptor alpha, has shown clinical benefit in small trials in children with ASD, but the underlying biology is incompletely understood. In this pre-specified biomarker substudy of a completed double-blind placebo-controlled trial (NCT02000284; NCT01602016), children with ASD received leucovorin (2 mg/kg/day, maximum 50 mg/day) or a matched placebo for 12 weeks. Peripheral blood mononuclear cell respiration was measured by extracellular flux with a graded 2,3-dimethoxy-1,4-naphthoquinone (DMNQ) challenge (38 participants; 17 leucovorin, 21 placebo) and plasma thiol-methylation metabolites were measured pre- and post-treatment (42 participants; 18 leucovorin, 24 placebo). Leucovorin increased basal, ATP-linked, proton-leak, maximal, and reserve respiration relative to the placebo (Group × Visit p ≤ 0.012, all q ≤ 0.012; Cohen's d 0.48-0.92); there was no evidence that the treatment effect varied across the tested DMNQ concentrations. In exploratory moderator analyses, folate receptor alpha autoantibody (FRAA) status modified the effect on maximal respiratory capacity and reserve capacity (both p < 0.001), with the largest gains in FRAA-positive children receiving leucovorin, and a history of neurodevelopmental regression modified the effect on basal, proton-leak and reserve respiration. The plasma SAM/SAH ratio increased (d = 0.77) and S-adenosylhomocysteine decreased (d = -0.67) on leucovorin; both were nominally significant (p = 0.020 and 0.050) but neither survived false-discovery-rate correction within the thiol family. The findings support the folate-mitochondrial-redox axis as a candidate therapeutic target in ASD and warrant replication in larger independent cohorts.

docs.title: Dual Role of CACNA1C/CaV1.2 in Cardiac and Neuropsychiatric Disease.
docs.text: The CACNA1C gene encodes the α1C subunit of voltage-gated CaV1.2 calcium channels, serving many pivotal functions throughout the body, including in the heart and brain. Clinical and genetic evidence implicates altered expression and/or function of CACNA1C/CaV1.2 in both cardiac and neuropsychiatric disease, including hypertension, cardiac arrhythmias, coronary artery disease, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, and autism. Gain-of-function mutations in CACNA1C cause Timothy syndrome, a potentially lethal multi-organ disorder with severe cardiac and neuropsychiatric defects. Conversely, the complete loss of Cacna1c is lethal in mice. The development of viable mouse and rat models with Cacna1c haploinsufficiency has allowed us to study the consequences of reduced expression and function of Cacna1c/CaV1.2 for heart and brain function from the molecular and cellular to the behavioral level. We review recent findings from these rodent models, revealing (i) alterations in behavior and (ii) in neuronal and non-neuronal function, as well as (iii) an impaired ability of the heart and its cardiomyocytes to adapt to (sympathetic) stress. Results lend further support to the notion that CACNA1C/CaV1.2 dysfunction represents a common link between cardiac and neuropsychiatric disorders and that appropriately targeting CACNA1C/CaV1.2 in selected patients may hold the promise of treating both conditions effectively with a single drug.

docs.title: Epigenetic Hierarchies in Autism from Folate-SAM Metabolism to LSD1 and G9a.
docs.text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a diverse neurodevelopmental condition involving interactions among genetic, environmental, metabolic, immune, synaptic, and epigenetic factors. This review explores whether disruptions in folate-dependent one-carbon metabolism and S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) availability may increase epigenetic susceptibility in specific ASD subgroups based on biological criteria. This narrative, hypothesis-driven review synthesizes selected peer-reviewed literature encompassing human studies, animal models, cell systems, and biochemical research. Findings including decreased methylation capacity, altered DNA methylation, and abnormal histone methylation have been reported in ASD and related neurodevelopmental conditions. Nonetheless, evidence strength varies considerably depending on phenotype, tissue type, developmental stage, and experimental system. On this basis, a provisional SAM-dependent epigenetic hierarchy is proposed in which methyltransferases may differ in vulnerability to metabolic stress according to enzyme kinetics, subcellular context, developmental timing, and compensatory regulation. This model is conceptual rather than an established mechanism demonstrated uniformly across ASD. Clinical and translational findings are interpreted cautiously. Evidence for folinic acid is strongest in selected subgroups such as folate receptor alpha autoantibody-positive ASD and cerebral folate deficiency-related presentations, whereas LSD1/KDM1A and G9a/EHMT1/2 modulation remains largely preclinical. Overall, the review argues that folate-SAM-related epigenetic dysregulation may represent one contributory pathway in some ASD subgroups and provides a framework for future mechanistic and stratified therapeutic studies.

docs.title: Genetic Convergence of Autism Spectrum Disorder and Epilepsy: From Molecular Mechanisms to Precision Therapeutics.
docs.text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and epilepsy frequently co-occur, with the clinical overlap particularly evident in individuals with intellectual disability, developmental impairment, and genetically defined neurodevelopmental disorders. Advances in genomic diagnostics have revealed substantial genetic and molecular convergence between ASD and epilepsy. This convergence encompasses both recurrent copy-number variants (CNVs), including 15q11-q13, 16p11.2, and 22q11.2 rearrangements, and sequence-level alterations in genes implicated in both epilepsy and ASD-related neurodevelopmental phenotypes, including SCN1A, SCN2A, GRIN2A, SYNGAP1, STXBP1, TSC1/TSC2, MECP2, and UBE3A. These diverse genetic alterations affect gene dosage, ion-channel function, synaptic organization and neurotransmission, intracellular signaling, and gene regulation, ultimately converging on disruption of circuit homeostasis, excitation-inhibition regulation, synaptic plasticity, and network dynamics. Importantly, the relationship between epilepsy and ASD is neither uniform nor necessarily causal: epileptic activity may aggravate neurodevelopmental dysfunction in some disorders, whereas in others, seizures and autistic features represent partially independent consequences of a shared genetic defect. This heterogeneity has major therapeutic implications. Emerging precision approaches increasingly incorporate variant-specific functional effects and include ion-channel modulation, pathway-directed treatments, metabolic correction, and gene- or RNA-targeted therapies. However, successful seizure control does not necessarily translate into normalization of neurodevelopmental outcomes, emphasizing the importance of developmental timing and of distinguishing seizure-directed benefit from modification of the underlying neurodevelopmental disorder. This review integrates clinical, genetic, molecular, cellular, and network-level evidence linking ASD and epilepsy and examines how these convergent mechanisms may guide precision therapeutics and future early-intervention strategies.

docs.title: From Signal to Memory: A Proposed Adaptive Hierarchy Linking Autism-Associated Genes to Sensory Homeostasis.
docs.text: Every nervous system must preserve sensitivity to change while reducing responses to constancy. This review defines that adaptive objective as sensory homeostasis: the process through which familiar information recedes while unexpected or biologically important events remain salient. Its disruption is particularly relevant to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), in which sensory abnormalities occur across multiple modalities. Large-scale sequencing studies have identified hundreds of ASD-associated genes spanning neuronal excitability, synaptic function, intracellular signaling, transcription, and chromatin regulation. This hypothesis-driven narrative review asks whether the established functions of independently identified ASD-associated genes support a directional framework through which genetic vulnerability could compromise sensory homeostasis. Beginning with a prespecified Autism Sequencing Consortium-derived set of 185 ASD-associated genes, and separately classifying complementary genetic and mechanistic evidence, the review organizes a bounded subset into three functional levels: generation and spatial organization of intracellular Ca2+ signals; interpretation of those signals by electrical, biochemical, synaptic, and transcriptional decoders; and stabilization of selected responses through transcriptional and chromatin-regulatory mechanisms that establish adaptive cellular memory. The resulting 44-gene core contains 32 of the 185 members distributed across all three levels and identifies IP3R-mediated endoplasmic-reticulum Ca2+ release as an important, but not exclusive, Level 1 convergence mechanism in signal generation. The proposed framework predicts distinct proximal defects that converge on abnormal response trajectories across repeated stimulation, providing a testable connection among ASD genetics, adaptive cellular memory, and sensory phenotype.

docs.title: Shared Genetic and Regulatory Architecture of Congenital Heart Disease and Autism Spectrum Disorder Revealed by Cross-Tissue Multi-Omic Integration.
docs.text: Background: Congenital heart disease (CHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) co-occur more frequently than expected, suggesting shared developmental susceptibility. We aimed to identify cross-tissue molecular candidates linking cardiac and neurodevelopmental abnormalities. Methods: CHD- and ASD-associated genes were curated from MalaCards and SFARI Gene, and their intersection was defined as the CHD- and ASD-associated gene set (CAGES). Shared gene enrichment was assessed against the human protein-coding genome. CHD and ASD genome-wide association data were integrated with heart and brain cis-expression quantitative trait loci using Bayesian colocalization and summary data-based Mendelian randomization with HEIDI testing. Candidates were further evaluated using bulk transcriptomics, six machine learning feature selection methods, independent cohorts, and scTenifoldKnk virtual knockout analyses in developing human heart and cerebral cortex. Results: Seventy-three genes were shared between CHD and ASD. CHD7 showed suggestive colocalization for CHD and ASD, while lower genetically predicted CHD7 expression was associated with higher odds of both disorders, with nonsignificant HEIDI tests. MEF2C was downregulated in tetralogy of Fallot myocardium and selected by all six ASD machine learning methods, with consistently lower expression in ASD. CAGES-derived signatures discriminated independent CHD, ASD cord blood, and cortical cohorts. CHD7 virtual knockout analysis identified MEF2C as a computationally predicted regulatory candidate in the prenatal brain, particularly in late-fetal excitatory neurons and intermediate progenitor cells, with cell-type-specific predicted effects also observed in the developing heart. Conclusions: CHD and ASD share molecular susceptibility involving pleiotropic developmental mechanisms. CHD7 and MEF2C emerge as connected cross-tissue candidates across complementary genetically informed, transcriptomic, and developmental regulatory analyses, highlighting prenatal neuronal populations and developmental windows for investigating the heart-brain axis.

docs.title: Association of Copy Number Variations in PTEN with Autism Spectrum Disorder.
docs.text: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with a strong genetic basis. While copy number variations (CNVs) significantly contribute to ASD risk, the specific role of individual genes within these variants remains unclear. This study investigates the contribution of CNVs in the PTEN gene to ASD pathophysiology by integrating population-level genetic analysis with multi-dimensional biological evidence. Methods: The biological plausibility of PTEN in ASD was first assessed using public multi-omics data, including tissue expression profiles, protein-protein interaction networks, and published cell-type-specific differential-expression data derived from single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Subsequently, a group-matched case-control study was conducted in a Han Chinese population (121 ASD cases and 110 controls) to evaluate the association between PTEN CNVs and ASD susceptibility. One-way ANOVA was performed to compare the differences in ASD clinical phenotype scores among groups with different CNV types of PTEN. Results: Integrative biological analyses revealed that PTEN is enriched in ASD-relevant brain regions (e.g., cerebellum) and exhibits cell-type-specific expression in neurons and glia. Furthermore, protein network analysis confirmed its central position within the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, a critical regulator of neurodevelopment. In the Han Chinese population, no significant association was detected between PTEN CNVs and ASD risks or clinical phenotype scores. Conclusions:PTEN CNVs may not be independently associated with ASD, but may contribute to susceptibility through broader neurodevelopmental networks and molecular pathways.

docs.title: Mapping and visualizing global research trends in gut microbiota and autism spectrum disorder: A bibliometric analysis (2015-2024).
docs.text: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder with increasing research interest in its association with the gut microbiota. However, the knowledge structure and development of this field have not been systematically analyzed. Methods: We conducted a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of English-language publications related to ASD and gut microbiota from 2015 to 2024 using the Web of Science Core Collection. We used the bibliometrix package in R, VOSviewer, and CiteSpace for analysis, focusing on publication trends, geographic and institutional contributions, prominent authors and journals, citation patterns, keyword dynamics, and thematic clusters. Results: A total of 1309 publications were included, involving corresponding authors from 64 countries or regions. The annual number of publications steadily increased from 2015 to 2022, followed by a slight decline in 2023 and a partial rebound in 2024, with the US and China contributing the most. Leading authors and teams were primarily based in North America and Europe. Thematic evolution revealed a shift from early mechanistic research to intervention-focused topics, such as short-chain fatty acids, fecal microbiota transplantation, and probiotics. Conclusion: Research on ASD and gut microbiota is progressing from theoretical exploration toward early-stage translational research, with increasing investigation of potential clinical applications. Future studies should emphasize multi-omics integration, mechanistic validation, and international collaboration. This bibliometric analysis offers a comprehensive overview to inform and guide future research in this rapidly evolving field.

docs.title: Anaesthetic Management of a Child with Chromosome 7q32.1 Microdeletion Undergoing Ligation of Patent Processus Vaginalis.
docs.text: Presentation: A six-year-old boy with chromosome 7q32.1 microdeletion, autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, hypotonia and asthma presented for elective ligation of a patent processus vaginalis under general anaesthesia. Diagnosis: Chromosome 7q32.1 microdeletion is a rare genetic disorder with developmental, behavioural and neuromuscular features. Coexisting reactive airway disease and autism spectrum disorder heighten the risk of perioperative respiratory adverse events (PRAEs) and complicate induction and emergence. Treatment: A perioperative strategy minimising airway stimulation and preserving spontaneous ventilation was employed. Anaesthesia was induced with sevoflurane in oxygen; a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) was used instead of endotracheal intubation, and neuromuscular blockade was avoided. The perioperative course was uneventful, with no respiratory complications. Discussion: Use of a supraglottic airway with maintenance of spontaneous ventilation, and a calm behaviourally tailored approach, facilitated safe anaesthesia in this child. This case adds to the limited literature on the anaesthetic implications of chromosome 7q32.1 microdeletion.

docs.title: Environmental and genetic interactions in autism spectrum disorder: a literature review with a focus on air pollution.
docs.text: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition which is associated with complex interactions between genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures. More recently, air pollution has been investigated as a modifiable risk factor and contributor to the neurodevelopmental outcomes of the disorder. This review focuses on the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region and discusses genetic, immunologic, and epigenetic findings that help explain how pollutants, including particulate matter (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀), nitrogen oxides, ozone, and dioxins, contribute to the pathogenesis of ASD and its specific involvement in neuronal pathways. Many pollutants have been found to increase oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and endocrine disruption which alters DNA methylation and histone modification patterns. The pathology of this involves activation of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) and its downstream CYP1A1/CYP1B1 pathways which link environmental to altered gene expression and neural circuits. Current studies have shown that prenatal and early postnatal exposures are critical windows in which air pollutants can impair synaptogenesis, microglial regulation, and neurotransmitter balance. Significantly, sex-specific differences further modulate susceptibility, with males demonstrating heightened vulnerability due to hormonal and immune interactions. While progress has been made in uncovering these mechanisms, challenge in establishing causality and addressing diagnostic biases persists. Future directions should integrate longitudinal cohorts, omics-based biomarkers, and machine-learning models to clarify exposure-response relationships and guide personalized prevention strategies. Understanding how environmental and genetic factors converge to disrupt neurodevelopment is essential to mitigating ASD risk in increasingly polluted environments.
docs.venue: Environmental health : a global access science source

docs.title: Whole-exome sequencing in a Turkish autism spectrum disorder cohort: a retrospective study of molecular diagnostic yield in isolated and complex presentations.
docs.text: Background: Whole-exome sequencing (WES) can identify molecular etiologies in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), particularly when ASD occurs with developmental delay/intellectual disability (DD/ID), epilepsy, dysmorphism, congenital anomalies, or neuroimaging abnormalities. Data on WES yield and candidate-gene findings in Turkish ASD cohorts remain limited. We assessed molecular diagnostic yield and variant spectrum in a Turkish clinical ASD cohort, with comparison of isolated and complex ASD presentations. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 320 individuals with ASD evaluated by WES between 2020 and 2025. Patients were classified as having isolated or complex ASD based on co-occurring neurodevelopmental, neurological, dysmorphic, congenital, or systemic findings. Variants were interpreted using ACMG/AMP criteria. Established molecular diagnoses required pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants associated with OMIM-defined disorders or occurring in genes with definitive, strong, or moderate ClinGen evidence for a neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD). Categorical comparisons used two-sided Fisher's exact test. Results: Established molecular diagnoses were identified in 104/320 patients (32.5%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 27.4-37.9%), including 2/22 patients with isolated ASD (9.1%; 95% CI, 1.1-29.2%) and 102/298 patients with complex ASD (34.2%; 95% CI, 28.9-39.9%; p = 0.017). An additional 12 patients had P/LP variants in candidate or emerging genes, resulting in an overall P/LP finding rate of 116/320 (36.3%; 95% CI, 31.0-41.8%). Variants of uncertain significance were identified in 147 patients, while no ASD/NDD-related variant was identified in 57 patients. Conclusions: WES supports etiological clarification in clinically complex ASD. Established molecular diagnoses were substantially more frequent in complex than isolated ASD. Candidate and emerging gene findings should be reported separately and interpreted as hypothesis-generating.

docs.title: Integrating multi-omics data through deep learning with applications to autism risk gene prioritization.
docs.text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable neurodevelopmental disorder. Advances in genetic research, particularly whole-exome sequencing studies, have identified an increasing number of ASD risk genes, especially through large-effect rare variant analyses. However, current rare-variant studies still have limited power to recover the full spectrum of ASD risk genes, leaving a substantial gap between known genes and the estimated genetic architecture of ASD. To address this challenge, we developed Deep-MOTIFs (Multi-Omics inTegratIon For autiSm), a Bayesian-guided positive-unlabeled deep learning framework for multi-omics integration that combines genetic, transcriptomic, and protein-interaction evidence for genome-wide ASD risk-gene prioritization. Deep-MOTIFs achieved stronger performance than existing methods across held-out ASD gene prediction, top-ranked prioritization, positive-label efficiency, and label-noise robustness analyses. Functional enrichment and genome-wide decile analyses further supported the biological relevance of the top-ranked candidates, showing convergence on ASD-related phenotypic annotations and synaptic, neurodevelopmental, and chromatin-regulatory mechanisms. Together, these results support Deep-MOTIFs as a robust framework for ASD risk-gene prioritization under incomplete supervision. Source code is available at: https://github.com/shan-team/Deep-MOTIFs.

docs.title: Effect of Probiotics on GI Symptom Management in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Clinical Trials.
docs.text: Autism spectrum disorder has increased worldwide over the past few decades. Medical comorbidities are common in patients with ASD, with gastrointestinal (GI) diseases being especially common. Involvement of the gut-brain axis that communicates between the enteric and central nervous systems has been confirmed by several studies that have reported abnormal microbiota profiles in ASD subjects. In this review, a systematic database search was conducted. Six trials were included in the subgroup analysis that compared probiotic therapy with single or multiple strains to a placebo with respect to gastrointestinal severity index. The pooled effect size model revealed a slight decrease in gastrointestinal symptoms that favored probiotic supplementation (SMD = -0.189; 95% CI = -0.398 to 0.020; Z = -1.773, p = 0.07; I2 = 39.4%). There was a moderate level of heterogeneity among the included studies. Additionally, the effects of single-strain and multiple-strain probiotic formulations were compared to their respective placebo groups using subgroup analysis. The results demonstrated that single-strain probiotic medication reduced gastrointestinal symptoms when compared to the placebo group. However, there was no statistically significant difference between multiple-strain probiotic therapy and a placebo. To accurately establish the therapeutic effects of probiotics on ASD, more randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies are required.

docs.title: Entrainment of prefrontal theta synchrony increases interbrain coupling and enhances social interaction in mouse models of autism.
docs.text: Social interaction requires the integration of information about self, other, and shared context. One of the proposed mechanisms supporting this coordination is interbrain synchrony - correlated neural activity between interacting individuals - yet its role in shaping social behavior remains unresolved. Here, we show that theta band synchrony in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is closely linked to social interaction in mice and often precedes its onset. In male Shank2 mutant mice, a genetic model of social dysfunction, mPFC interbrain synchrony was diminished, along with a reduced population of mPFC neurons encoding multiple dimensions of social information. Optogenetic entrainment of theta synchrony was accompanied by increased interbrain coupling and social interaction in male Shank2-/- and Tbr1+/K228E mutant mice, two well-established genetic models of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). These findings identify prefrontal theta synchrony as a neural substrate that supports social behavior and provide a framework for understanding how coordinated neural activity across brains contributes to social interaction.

docs.title: Biochemical correlates of social anxiety in subjects with autism spectrum conditions.
docs.text: Background: Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is a common and debilitating condition marked by intense fear of negative evaluation in social situations. It often co-occurs with other psychiatric disorders, and in particular Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). The exact cause of SAD is unclear, though biological, environmental, and genetic factors are believed to contribute. Recent research highlights the involvement of neuropeptides, neurohormones, and immune system components in SAD development, suggesting complex interactions between psychological and biological factors, with a growing focus on inflammation's role. This study aimed to investigate potential biochemical correlates of SAD in individuals with ASD, their first-degree relatives (BAP group), and healthy controls (HCs), focusing on inflammatory markers, neuropeptides, and growth factors. Methods: Twenty-four adults with ASD, their relatives, and HCs, for a total of 72 participants, were assessed. Biochemical parameters were analyzed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA), and social anxiety symptoms were evaluated via the Social Phobia Spectrum-Self Report (SHY-SR) questionnaire. Results: Individuals with ASD exhibited significantly higher SHY-SR scores compared to the BAP and HCs. Subjects in the ASD group tended to make greater use of anxiolytics in order to improve their social interaction skills. Additionally, a specific pattern of correlation and association was found between biochemical variables and specific SAD symptoms, suggesting a potential role of inflammatory pathways in SAD pathophysiology. Conclusions: Our results confirm the presence of greater social phobic symptoms in subjects with ASD, and support the hypothesis of a role of the inflammatory cascade in the maintenance of the disorder.

docs.title: Variation in Primary Care Diagnostic Codes Used to Define Health Conditions for Research: Comparison of 45 Health Data Research UK Phenotype Library Codelists for Eight Health Conditions.
docs.text: Introduction: The use of electronic healthcare records (EHRs) has become standard practice in most healthcare settings in many countries. These can be utilised for research purposes by developing codelists to define cohorts and health conditions of interest. In the UK the Health Data Research UK (HDR UK) Phenotype Library is a resource where researchers can access multiple codelists deposited by other researchers for a range of medical conditions. Objectives: This paper examines variation in the published codelists in the HDR UK Phenotype Library for a number of conditions. Methods: We extracted codelists held within the HDR UK Phenotype Library for eight common conditions (asthma, autism, coronary heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, depression, hypertension, obesity, and type 2 diabetes). We categorised included codes as diagnostic, disease related, administrative, and unrelated to the condition. We explored the degree of agreement between codelists by estimating kappa statistics for codelists for each condition and category. Results: There were 48 published codelists for the eight conditions, with wide variation in the number of codes used to define each condition (for example from 39 to 247 codes in eight asthma codelists). Only codelists for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and depression consistently achieved fair (kappa 0.21-0.40) moderate agreement (kappa 0.41-0.60), with other conditions consistently achieving fair agreement at best. Agreement was higher for diagnostic codes, and lowest for administrative codes. Conclusions: The HDR UK Phenotype Library publishes researchers' codelists to facilitate greater transparency and replicability of studies. This study finds that agreement between codelists in terms of the codes included was low. Further research is needed to determine how such variation alters identification of which individuals have conditions of interest.
docs.venue: International journal of population data science

docs.title: Gut microbiota-mediated tryptophan metabolic dysregulation in the comorbidity of inflammatory bowel disease and autism spectrum disorder: mechanisms and research progress.
docs.text: The "microbiota-gut-brain axis" represents a critical link connecting various aspects of intestinal physiology, brain function, and behavioral performance. Among these, tryptophan metabolism abnormalities mediated by gut microbes through the gut-brain axis (GBA) have garnered widespread attention in the study of IBD-ASD comorbidity. This article reviews the current state of research on tryptophan metabolism abnormalities in IBD-ASD comorbidity, with a particular focus on the connection between peripheral and central tryptophan metabolic derangements mediated by gut microbes via the GBA. Furthermore, we summarize and analyze potential therapeutic targets and intervention strategies in this comorbid condition, integrating recent mechanistic studies and clinical evidence to provide a conceptual framework for understanding the potential mechanisms underlying IBD-ASD comorbidity. However, direct evidence from patients with confirmed IBD-ASD comorbidity remains limited at present, and further clinical studies are still needed to test this hypothesis.

docs.title: Prenatal exposure to maternal stress hormones and the risk of autism: a neuroendocrine-epigenetic scoping review.
docs.text: Maternal psychosocial stress during pregnancy is increasingly recognized as a factor capable of shaping fetal neurodevelopment through alterations in the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and placental regulatory systems. When maternal stress hormones, particularly cortisol, rise persistently during gestation, they may exceed the buffering capacity of the placenta, influencing fetal brain pathways implicated in social communication, sensory processing, and emotional regulation. Empirical evidence from prospective cohorts has shown that elevated maternal cortisol, altered diurnal HPA rhythms, and increased placental corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) trajectories are associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes relevant to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), although results remain heterogeneous across populations and methods [1-3]. This scoping review examines confirmed studies on prenatal stress hormones, placental enzymatic processes, epigenetic changes and their relation to stress, and the diagnosis of ASD and ASD-related traits on a continuum. Per the guidance of the Joanna Briggs Institute and the Scoping Reviews and Mapping Approaches (PRISMA-ScR) framework, we cataloged the eligible studies on their research design, biomarkers, gestational periods, and outcomes by neurobiological processes, and of the children in question. Across studies with multiple methodologies, there is a consensus that disruptions in maternal HPA axis functioning and placental signaling contribute to early changes in the trajectory of ASD development, with the moderating variables of fetal sex, maternal mental health and environmental adversity. While there is no compelling evidence of a causal relationship, the strength and consistency of the proposed mechanisms support the idea that prenatal HPA and epigenetic processes play an important role in shaping the development of ASD. The review highlights the importance of cross study harmonization of biomarkers, expanded longitudinal study designs with varied and several gestational samplings, and the need to pinpoint the timing, magnitude, and detail of the relationships between the stress biology of pregnancy and ASD with outcomes. Collectively, the findings present a framework and strengthened the linkage of the maternal stress physiology to the neurodevelopment of the fetus. This provides a pathway for future mechanistic research and further applied research [10].

docs.title: Associations between Prenatal Exposure to Perchlorate, Thiocyanate, and Nitrate and Child Neurodevelopment in the MARBLES Study.
docs.text: Associations between prenatal exposure to perchlorate, thiocyanate, and nitrate and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remain largely unexplored. We investigated these associations in the MARBLES cohort, a prospective cohort with an elevated familial likelihood of ASD. A total of 310 mothers provided 1916 urine samples during pregnancy, and their children were classified at age 3 years as typically developing (TD), ASD, or non-TD (developmental concerns not meeting ASD diagnostic criteria). We estimated relative risks for ASD and non-TD compared with TD using Poisson regression and assessed mixture effects using quantile G-computation and Bayesian kernel machine regression. Overall and mixture analyses showed no significant associations between prenatal exposure to these NIS inhibitors and the child neurodevelopmental outcomes. However, stratified analyses identified several context-specific associations according to child sex, trimester of exposure, maternal urinary iodine concentration, and passive smoking status, some of which remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction. These findings suggest that susceptibility to prenatal exposure to perchlorate, thiocyanate, and nitrate may vary across population subgroups and exposure windows. Although these subgroup-specific associations should be considered hypothesis generating, they highlight the need for future studies integrating thyroid biomarkers and mechanistic approaches to better understand thyroid-related pathways underlying child neurodevelopment.

docs.title: Association of Heat, Cold, and Ambient Pollution in the First 1000 Days of Life with Autism Spectrum Disorder Risk Indicators in Two-Year-Olds. Findings from the ELFE National Birth Cohort.
docs.text: Early life is a vulnerable period to environmental exposures that may be associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We investigated associations between prenatal and postnatal exposure to weekly averages of temperature and air pollutants (PM2.5, PM10, NO2) with autism screening scores (based on the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised version) in 12,139 2-year-olds from the French ELFE birth cohort. Exposures were based on daily outdoor predictions at 1 km resolution (200 m in large urban areas for temperature and NO2). Relationships were modeled with confounder-adjusted distributed lag nonlinear models and generalized linear models.
